What must be controlled: The complete melt recipe, acceptable residual elements and recovery of the Mg addition
What the evidence does—and does not—esta: Some users accept Mg-Al alloys: Platts specifies an AM50A/AM60B-based assessment for aluminum users. Buying 99.99% Mg is not a universal requirement.

What must be controlled: Specified alloy composition, trace impurities and casting quality
What the evidence does—and does not—esta: AZ91D is an alloy product, not a “99.9% Mg” grade. Supplier ranges are illustrative; the customer’s ingot and finished-part specifications must be distinguished.

What must be controlled: Composition plus particle-size distribution and particle form
What the evidence does—and does not—esta: Luxfer publishes both chemistry and size/form options and lists steel desulfurization among uses. The brochure does not disclose an individual steelmaker’s acceptance limits.

What must be controlled: Suitability of reducing metal and returned chloride for the internal process
What the evidence does—and does not—esta: UKTMP has a documented Mg/MgCl2 loop. Current customer-specific impurity ceilings were not located; no blanket “titanium grade = 99.95%” assumption is made.

What must be controlled: Anode chemistry and measured electrochemical performance
What the evidence does—and does not—esta: Anodes are designed to be consumed during protection. Composition alone does not establish current efficiency or service life in a particular environment.

What must be controlled: Approved material, consistent lots, qualification and traceability
What the evidence does—and does not—esta: In the USITC’s historical survey, 10 of 11 purchasers required supplier qualification; reported times ranged from seven days to two years. This is historical survey evidence, not a universal or current lead time.
